title: Lost in Sequence: Do Large Language Models Understand Sequential Recommendation?

problem.claim: LLM-based recommendation models are used in sequential recommendation, where users' item interaction sequences contain sequential information.

gap.claim: Whether LLM-based recommendation models understand the sequential information in users' item interaction sequences has been largely overlooked.

contributions.claim: Existing LLM-based recommendation models do not fully capture sequential information during training and inference.
LLM-SRec integrates sequential information into LLMs by distilling user representations from a pre-trained CF-SRec model into LLMs.
LLM-SRec trains only a few lightweight MLPs instead of fine-tuning the LLM.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments show that existing LLM-based recommendation models do not fully capture sequential information during training and inference.
The authors report that extensive experiments show LLM-SRec improves LLMs' ability to understand users' item interaction sequences and improves recommendation performance.
The authors report state-of-the-art performance for LLM-SRec while training only a few lightweight MLPs.

narrative_sequence.summary: LLMs are presented as promising tools for recommendation because of their textual understanding and context-awareness.
The extent to which LLM-based recommendation models understand sequential information has been overlooked.
Experiments indicate that existing models do not fully capture sequential information during training and inference.
The paper introduces LLM-SRec, which distills user representations from a pre-trained CF-SRec model into an LLM.
The authors report improved recommendation performance and state-of-the-art performance with training limited to a few lightweight MLPs.

source_observation.claim: Existing LLM-based recommendation models may not fully use sequential information even when trained and evaluated in sequential recommendation settings.

interpretation.claim: Applying an LLM to sequential data does not by itself ensure that the model represents sequence information.

application.claim: Evaluate whether a model uses sequence information during both training and inference rather than relying only on overall recommendation performance.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this observation generalizes beyond the evaluated LLM-based recommendation models or settings.

source_observation.claim: Distilling user representations from a pre-trained collaborative-filtering sequential recommender into an LLM is reported to improve sequential understanding and recommendation performance.

interpretation.claim: Representations from a specialized sequential model may provide a lightweight way to inject sequential information into an LLM.

application.claim: Consider representation distillation and lightweight adaptation when full LLM fine-tuning is impractical.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify the evaluated datasets, baselines, metrics, or conditions for the reported improvements and state-of-the-art performance.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the datasets, baselines, metrics, or experimental conditions.
The abstract does not describe the architecture or training details of the lightweight MLPs.
The abstract does not quantify the reported performance improvements.
